title: Unlocking the Second Half Advantage
about:
A keynote-driven course from The Platform Nigeria, taught by Prof. Modupe Elebute-Odunsi, consultant hematologist and founder and CEO of the Marcelle Ruth Cancer Centre and Specialist Hospital, the first one-stop cancer centre of its kind in West Africa.

After a world-class career in the UK, a quiet question would not leave her: is this all I am meant to do? This course follows how she answered it, trading acknowledgement for alignment, leaving security to build at home, and turning a hospital into a legacy of training and impact. It is a practical study in transition, for anyone who senses there is a second half still to live.
benefits:
• Recognise the niggle, the sense that you may be meant for more, and decide what to do with it
  • Tell the difference between success measured by titles and comparison, and success measured by meaning
  • Act on clarity even when it means leaving security, and plan a realistic bridge out
  • Build against the tide, assembling a team that holds the standard you set
  • Anchor your work in human impact, not just infrastructure
  • Think in legacy: train others, lift your peers, and start before you feel ready

steps.title: The question that will not go away

item.content:
Prof. Elebute-Odunsi opens with the question that visits even the most successful people: is this all I am meant to do?

In this lesson

  • Why success does not silence the niggling question
  • The choice it forces: respond, or let it ride
  • How that choice shapes your second half

A Surulere girl in a household of two professors, she traces her calling to a childhood moment at her grandmother's bedside.

In this lesson

  • Roots on the University of Lagos campus
  • The bedside moment that planted a calling
  • The wish that became a decision to become a doctor

steps.title: Work hard, be bold: the early years

item.content:
She is candid that the sciences did not come easily, and that effort and boldness mattered more than raw talent.

In this lesson

  • Making the extra effort when it does not come easily
  • Given what you need: faith in the journey
  • Co-founding a sickle cell clinic as a fifth-year student

steps.title: Success as a destination, and the first crack

item.content:
For fourteen years the title of hematologist was the whole measure of success, until the job she was sure of slipped away.

In this lesson

  • Treating a title as the destination
  • The first consultant interview she did not win
  • The first crack: being acknowledged is not the same as belonging

Leading a rare-disease centre at King's College and developing a drug, she measured success against her peers, and built a foundation of excellence.

In this lesson

  • The scoreboard trap of comparing yourself to others
  • Turning her own research into a treatment
  • The NHS discipline she would carry home

Around her fiftieth birthday she named the gap: nothing was missing, yet achievement and meaning had stopped matching.

In this lesson

  • The disconnect between her idea of success and real meaning
  • The one thing: go and do it at home
  • Serving her real patients, her own people

item.content:
Clarity came quickly; acting on it did not. Handing back her licence took courage, and a real cost.

In this lesson

  • What do you do with the question once you have it
  • The GMC asking: are you really sure
  • The cost of leaving security as a wife and mother of five

steps.title: God orders your steps, and the four-year bridge

item.content:
She frames the leap in faith, then shows the practical bridge that made it possible.

In this lesson

  • Believing that every step is part of the journey
  • A gracious arrangement to work part-time
  • Four years of groundwork before coming home

steps.title: Going home when everyone was leaving

item.content:
She returned to Lagos at the end of 2019, into COVID and a wave of professionals leaving the country.

In this lesson

  • Choosing alignment, and the sacrifices it required
  • Why a hospital is really about its team
  • Building three buildings while almost everyone advised against it

steps.title: One building, one team, one standard

item.content:
The centre brought all of a patient's care under one roof, and she is clear about what made it work.

In this lesson

  • One-stop care instead of chasing labs across the city
  • A team that believes and holds the standard
  • The support behind the founder that made it possible

steps.title: Why it matters: the human cost

item.content:
Behind the growth statistics are families kept whole, the real reason the work matters.

In this lesson

  • From five staff to over a hundred, and thousands of patients
  • Children who no longer have to fly abroad for care
  • The disruption that fragmented, distant care does to families

steps.title: Stepping stones and the training legacy

item.content:
She reframes even the hospital as a stepping stone toward a larger legacy of training.

In this lesson

  • Respond to the call, and the assignment grows
  • The buildings as a stepping stone, not the destination
  • The first private hospital to train oncology residents in Nigeria

From a small lunch idea grew a movement, and she closes with a direct charge to you.

In this lesson

  • Why women in the sector must lift each other
  • The Women in Healthcare Network, from twenty to hundreds
  • The charge: if the question keeps coming, just go for it
